# Reinforcement and Imitation Learning {#ml-reinforcement-learning .ml-prep}

At the intersection the ego car can brake now or keep rolling and brake later. The choice affects the next gap, what the cyclist sees, and which actions will still be possible. A **policy** maps the current information to an action or a distribution over actions. Learning to make successive choices requires accounting for those future consequences.

[Value functions](#ml-bellman) · [Policy gradients](#ml-policy-gradients) · [Choosing a training setup](#ml-rl-data) · [ChauffeurNet](#ml-chauffeurnet) · [Waymax](#ml-waymax) · [RL fine-tuning](#ml-rl-finetuning)

## From one reward to a value function {#ml-bellman}

A **Markov decision process** specifies states \(s\), actions \(a\), a transition distribution \(P(s'\mid s,a)\), rewards \(r\), and a discount \(0\leq\gamma\leq1\). The Markov assumption says the state contains the history needed to predict what happens next given an action. In traffic, a single camera frame rarely does. A partially observed policy can use a history of observations or a belief distribution over hidden states. Even a long history may leave uncertainty about a cyclist's intent.

The **return** \(G_t=r_t+\gamma r_{t+1}+\gamma^2r_{t+2}+\cdots\) measures cumulative reward. With \(\gamma=0.9\), toy rewards \((-1,0,4)\) give \(G_0=2.24\). The **state value** \(V^\pi(s)\) is expected return when policy \(\pi\) starts at \(s\). The **action value** \(Q^\pi(s,a)\) fixes the first action, then follows \(\pi\). The one-step decomposition gives the Bellman expectation equation

\[
Q^\pi(s,a)=\mathbb E\!\left[r+\gamma V^\pi(s')\mid s,a\right],
\qquad V^\pi(s)=\sum_a\pi(a\mid s)Q^\pi(s,a).
\]

The sum is for discrete actions. The **advantage** \(A^\pi(s,a)=Q^\pi(s,a)-V^\pi(s)\) tells us how much better an action is than the policy's usual choice in that state. [Definitions and Bellman equations](https://spinningup.openai.com/en/latest/spinningup/rl_intro.html)

**Work a value update.** In a toy discrete-action Q-learning problem, suppose \(Q(s,\mathrm{brake})=1\), the observed reward is \(-1\), and the next state's largest estimated action value is 4. The target is \(-1+0.9(4)=2.6\). A learning rate of 0.25 moves the estimate to \(1+0.25(2.6-1)=1.4\). This **bootstraps** from another estimate. At a true terminal state, future value is zero. A recording that ends solely because its time window expired may still have future value. Make that distinction when constructing targets.

## Learning an actor and a critic {#ml-policy-gradients}

A value-based agent can choose the action with the largest estimated value when the action set is small. With continuous steering and acceleration, a parameterized **actor** can produce an action directly. A **critic** estimates the return or advantage used to train the actor. A policy-gradient update increases the log probability of sampled actions in proportion to their advantage. For a trajectory with probability \(p_\theta(\tau)\), the identity \(\nabla p=p\nabla\log p\) converts a gradient of expected return into an expectation over sampled trajectories. With fixed environment dynamics, the trainable factors are the policy's action probabilities.

For **REINFORCE**, a full sampled return supplies the weight. Subtracting a baseline that depends on the state but not the sampled action preserves the expected policy gradient and can reduce its variance. The baseline's expected contribution vanishes because \(\sum_a \pi(a\mid s)\nabla\log\pi(a\mid s)=\nabla\sum_a\pi(a\mid s)=0\). A critic's one-step estimate \(r+\gamma V(s')-V(s)\) often has less variance, but critic errors bias the estimate. Generalized advantage estimation averages discounted sequences of these residuals, trading variance against reliance on the critic. [Schulman et al., advantage estimation](https://arxiv.org/abs/1506.02438)

**PPO by hand.** Store action probabilities from the policy that gathered a batch. For a sampled action define \(\rho=\pi_{\mathrm{new}}(a\mid s)/\pi_{\mathrm{old}}(a\mid s)\). PPO maximizes the average of the smaller of \(\rho A\) and \(\operatorname{clip}(\rho,1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon)A\). If an action with \(A=2\) rises from probability 0.20 to 0.30, \(\rho=1.5\). With \(\epsilon=0.2\) its contribution is \(\min(3,2.4)=2.4\). With \(A=-2\) the same probability increase gives \(\min(-3,-2.4)=-3\), so a harmful move is still penalized. Clipping limits the incentive on particular samples. Track actual policy divergence, entropy and returns because other samples and shared parameters still move the policy. [Schulman et al., §3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1707.06347)

## Choose the learning setup to match the data {#ml-rl-data}

| Available experience | What to learn | What can go wrong |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Recorded expert states and actions | **Behavior cloning (BC)** maximizes the probability of demonstrated actions. | A small error moves the policy to states with little expert coverage. |
| States visited by the learner, plus expert labels | **DAgger** aggregates expert corrections at those visited states. | Querying an expert can be expensive. A logged action from a different state is a poor label. |
| A simulator you can step and score | **Online RL** gathers new trajectories as the policy changes. | The policy can discover unrealistic responses that inflate reward. |
| A fixed log with rewards | **Offline RL** estimates values or policies from existing transitions. | Maximizing over actions with little data can pick an overestimated, unsupported action. |

Conservative Q-learning adds pressure to reduce estimated values for actions relative to those supported by the data. Policy regularization can also keep decisions close to the logged behavior. Both can suppress legitimate improvements when the data contain few good actions. Compare against cloning at the same data budget and report results by action coverage. **On-policy** means training on experience from the policy being updated, up to the algorithm's permitted reuse. **Off-policy** means a method can learn from a different behavior policy. “Off-policy” describes a relationship between policies, while “offline” describes the absence of new environment interaction. [DAgger](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v15/ross11a.html) · [Conservative Q-Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.04779)

**Reward design exercise.** Give one point for each metre of route progress and a penalty for a collision. An agent can earn progress too quickly by cutting corners, or avoid collisions by parking if the penalty dominates. Define events consistently, test the reward on hand-constructed trajectories, and log each component separately. For evaluation, use independently specified collision, road departure, progress and jerk metrics. Inspect runs with the best returns as well as the worst ones. A simulator flaw can make a high-return trajectory an especially revealing failure.

## ChauffeurNet and learning to recover {#ml-chauffeurnet}

Bansal, Krizhevsky and Ogale (RSS 2019) ask how a driver trained on good demonstrations learns to recover from its own mistakes. Imagine a car entering a bend 40 centimetres too far right. A training set full of perfectly centred turns contains many examples of ordinary steering and few examples of steering back. With each predicted action, the learner changes its next observation. This mismatch between training and deployment states is called **covariate shift**. [ChauffeurNet, introduction and §III](https://www.roboticsproceedings.org/rss15/p31.pdf#page=1)

The input is a bird’s-eye drawing of roads, moving objects, signals, motion history and the intended route. A recurrent network predicts successive waypoints, which a controller converts to steering and acceleration. The authors shift the middle of an expert trajectory by up to 0.5 m in each coordinate, change its heading, and fit a smooth path back to the original endpoint. A training loss penalizes overlap between the predicted vehicle footprint and occupied or off-road regions. **Imitation dropout** switches off the imitation loss on a random fraction of examples, letting the environmental losses alone guide those updates. A separate trick hides past ego poses on some examples, encouraging the model to use signals such as a stop sign to decide when to brake. [ChauffeurNet, §§IV–V](https://www.roboticsproceedings.org/rss15/p31.pdf#page=5)

In Figure 6b, the basic cloning model M0 recovered in **0 of 20** deliberately offset starts on a curve. Models M3 and M4 recovered in **all 20**. Both combined perturbations, environmental losses and reduced emphasis on imitation. This comparison establishes the performance of the package. Table III’s intermediate variants help isolate individual changes. Figure 6c also shows a cost of M4’s behavior. In two high-relative-speed cases it tried to pass a slower car and grazed the road edge. These small, designed tests expose failure mechanisms. Population-level event rates would require representative sampling. [ChauffeurNet, Table III and Figure 6](https://www.roboticsproceedings.org/rss15/p31.pdf#page=7)

**Interview drill. Could recovery improve just because the model learned to drive slowly?** Train two otherwise identical models with and without synthetic perturbations. Start them on the same held-out curves with matched speeds and offsets. Record recovery within a fixed time, road departures, collisions and route progress. Include centred starts to measure any cost to ordinary driving. A stationary policy can score well on departures while failing recovery and progress.

## Waymax and the choice of simulated traffic {#ml-waymax}

Gulino et al. (NeurIPS 2023) build a simulator around a simple operation. Give it a scene and an action for each controlled participant, and it returns the next scene. The scene holds tracked object boxes, road geometry, signals and route information. A policy can use a **bicycle model**, a simplified car that advances under acceleration and steering curvature. Computing many independent scenes together on an accelerator makes it practical to repeat the same test under several traffic assumptions. This representation suits behavior research. Questions about camera glare require a sensor model. [Waymax, §§3–4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2310.08710#page=4)

Suppose the ego car brakes earlier than the recorded driver. Under **log playback**, the following car continues along its recorded time-stamped path. Under the **Intelligent Driver Model** (IDM) used here, it follows the logged path but adjusts speed using the gap and relative velocity ahead. Playback can create a collision that a human follower could have avoided. A consistently accommodating follower can also conceal poor gap selection. Traffic behavior is therefore part of the experimental setup. [Waymax, §§3.4–3.5](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2310.08710#page=5)

Table 5 crosses two training traffic models with two evaluation traffic models for a planner trained by deep Q-learning, which learns the expected future return of discrete actions. The IDM-trained planner’s collision rate went from **6.50% against IDM to 25.15% against playback**. For a planner trained against playback the corresponding rates were **4.91% and 8.67%**. All four measurements use the bicycle dynamics configuration. Switching evaluation traffic changes the measured rate for the very same planner. The authors suggest the IDM-trained planner may have learned to rely on other vehicles yielding. [Waymax, Table 5](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2310.08710#page=9)

**Interview drill. A simulator update halved collisions. Which component improved?** Freeze the old and new planners. Evaluate each against both traffic versions, using identical scenario starts and paired seeds. Count per-scenario collisions, off-road events and progress, then inspect the cases that changed. Add a held-out traffic model and examine whether the planner ordering persists. This design distinguishes a change in planner behavior from a change in what the evaluator demands.

## Reinforcement learning for simulated traffic agents {#ml-rl-finetuning}

Peng et al. (ECCV 2024) train the *surrounding road users* in a simulator. First a transformer learns to predict discrete motion tokens from logged histories. During pretraining it sees previous expert tokens, a practice called **teacher forcing**. During simulation it sees its own sampled tokens. A small early displacement can put a car in an unfamiliar position and eventually inside another vehicle. The authors fine-tune on complete sequences generated by the model itself. [Improving Agent Behaviors with RL Fine-tuning for Autonomous Driving, §§3–4](https://www.ecva.net/papers/eccv_2024/papers_ECCV/papers/03623.pdf#page=5)

At each step, each participant earns r = −d − λc, where d is its distance from the logged position, c is 1 if its box overlaps another box and 0 otherwise, and λ sets the collision penalty. An action’s **return** sums its current and later rewards, discounting later steps. The REINFORCE update weights the gradient of each sampled action’s log probability by its normalized return. An above-average outcome pushes the sampled choice to become more likely in that context. This update only requires the collision detector to return a score. Its derivative is unnecessary. [Peng et al., equations 2–5 and Algorithm 1](https://www.ecva.net/papers/eccv_2024/papers_ECCV/papers/03623.pdf#page=6)

Table 1 compares three ways to train the one-million-parameter model on the simulated-agent benchmark. The composite realism score was **0.490 after pretraining, 0.597 after RL fine-tuning, and 0.320 with RL alone**. Average displacement error fell from **6.332 m to 2.436 m** after fine-tuning. Table 2 shows why the collision penalty needs tuning. Increasing its weight from 2 to 10 reduced the collision *likelihood score* from 0.863 to 0.831 and increased displacement error from 2.436 m to 3.058 m. The score measures agreement with reference collision behavior. Reading 0.863 as the fraction of cars that collided would invert its meaning. [Peng et al., Tables 1–2](https://www.ecva.net/papers/eccv_2024/papers_ECCV/papers/03623.pdf#page=10)

**Interview drill. How would you tell whether traffic realism helps choose a planner?** Run identical planners in each traffic model. Compare the ordering of their mean returns with a reference ordering, and separately measure absolute return error. A simulator can preserve a ranking even when all returns are biased. The paper tries 64 search planners and uses log playback as its reference. Real drivers’ responses to those alternate plans are unobserved. A follow-up would retain the planner set, vary the reference traffic model, and report rank reversals with paired scenario uncertainty. [Peng et al., §5.2 and Tables 3–4](https://www.ecva.net/papers/eccv_2024/papers_ECCV/papers/03623.pdf#page=13)
